newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coalition agrees tax cut targets for 1998.
newsitem.headline: German coalition agrees tax cut targets for 1998.

text.p: Germany's centre-right coalition government on Thursday ended months of feuding and agreed to cut several key taxes in 1998 but affirmed that the budget would adhere to fiscal targets for Europe's single currency.
"We cannot do without a reduction of the burden of taxes and levies if we are to achieve more economic growth and employment," the coalition said in a position paper.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition of Christian Democrats (CDU) and Free Democrats (FDP) pledged to shave two points off the so-called solidarity tax to finance German unification, cutting it to 5.5 percent in 1998.

The cut in the solidarity tax and a reduction of corporate taxes would take effect on January 1, 1998, the paper said, adding that the cuts would be financed by commensurate reductions in state spending.

But commenting on its plans for a broader reform of the country's tax system, the coalition said only that such a reform would take effect on January 1, 1999 and that decisions would be taken in the next month on the details of the reform.

The paper also said the government was committed to maintaining the strict fiscal targets for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in its 1998 federal budget, saying: "The coalition will undertake all savings efforts to achieve an anti-inflationary stable budget in 1998 that meets the criteria of the Maastricht treaty and keeps the growth in state spending well below that of gross domestic product."
